claim: The HCP young adult cohort consists of healthy individuals without neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric, or neurologic disorders.
source: The HCP young adult cohort consists of healthy individuals without neurodevelopmental, neuropsychiatric, or neurologic disorders.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Materials and methods section describing the participant population.

claim: 907 right-handed healthy young adults were included in the study.
source: In the present study, we included a large cohort of 907 right-handed healthy young adults to assess whether and how PT lateralization of speech-related functional activation relates to its underlying structural asymmetries.
evidence: The sample size and handedness criteria are explicitly stated in the Introduction.

claim: The manual operation showed excellent interrater reliability for all PT measures.
source: As shown in Table 1, the manual operation showed excellent interrater reliability and imaging test-retest reproducibility for all PT measures.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by ICC values in Table 1.

claim: The interrater ICC values for PT measures ranged from 0.85 to 0.99.
source: As shown in Table 1, the interrater ICC values ranged from 0.85 to 0.99, indicating excellent interrater reliability for these measures.
evidence: ICC values are reported in Table 1 and described in the text.

claim: The imaging test-retest ICC values for PT measures ranged from 0.55 to 0.86.
source: As shown in Table 1, the imaging test-retest ICC values ranged from 0.55 to 0.86, indicating excellent test-retest reproducibility.
evidence: ICC values are reported in Table 1 and described in the text.

claim: Left HG duplication occurred in 229 subjects (25.3%).
source: Among these young adults, left and right HG duplications were identified in 229 and 263 subjects, respectively (occurrence rate: left, 25.3%, right, 29.0%).
evidence: The occurrence rate is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: Right HG duplication occurred in 263 subjects (29.0%).
source: Among these young adults, left and right HG duplications were identified in 229 and 263 subjects, respectively (occurrence rate: left, 25.3%, right, 29.0%).
evidence: The occurrence rate is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: 503 individuals had bilateral single HGs (L1/R1, 55.5%).
source: In terms of the HG gyrification pattern in both hemispheres, all subjects were divided into four groups: 503 individuals with bilateral sHGs (L1/R1, 55.5%), 175 individuals with left sHG but right dHG (L1/R2, 19.3%), 141 individuals with left dHG but right sHG (L2/R1, 15.6%), and 88 individuals with bilateral dHGs (L2/R2, 9.7%).
evidence: The distribution of HG gyrification patterns is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: Age and sex did not differ among the four HG gyrification pattern groups.
source: Age and sex did not differ among these four groups (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical tests in Table 2.

claim: Both left and right PTs showed significant group-level activation for all three contrasts within the auditory-language task.
source: Both left and right PTs showed significant group-level activation for all three contrasts (i.e. 'story – baseline,' 'math – baseline,' and 'story – math') within the task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating a strong functional involvement of both PTs in such auditory-language processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by activation maps in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Factor analysis of PT activation T values revealed two factors in each hemisphere: one representing speech perception and the other representing speech comprehension.
source: Factor analysis of the activation T values of the three contrasts revealed two factors in each hemisphere: one representing PT functional activation of speech perception and the other representing PT functional activation of speech comprehension.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the factor analysis approach.

claim: No significant correlations were found between PT functional and structural measures and behavioral language test scores.
source: We evaluated the correlation of functional and structural measures of the left and right PT with two available behavioral language test scores (the oral reading recognition test, measuring the ability to reade decoding; the picture vocabulary test, measuring the ability of linguistic comprehension), but found no significant results (all PFWE >0.05).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: Significant leftward PT lateralization was observed for both speech perception and comprehension in the L1/R1 group.
source: As shown in Figure 2, significant leftward PT lateralization was observed for both speech perception and comprehension in the L1/R1 (Cohen's d: speech perception = 0.35, speech comprehension = 0.36) and L1/R2 (Cohen's d: speech perception = 0.52, speech comprehension = 0.57) groups but not in the L2/R1 and L2/R2 groups (Supplementary file 1a), suggesting a specific influence of the HG gyrification pattern on speech-related functional lateralization of the PT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2 with effect sizes.

claim: Significant leftward PT lateralization was observed for both speech perception and comprehension in the L1/R2 group.
source: As shown in Figure 2, significant leftward PT lateralization was observed for both speech perception and comprehension in the L1/R1 (Cohen's d: speech perception = 0.35, speech comprehension = 0.36) and L1/R2 (Cohen's d: speech perception = 0.52, speech comprehension = 0.57) groups but not in the L2/R1 and L2/R2 groups (Supplementary file 1a), suggesting a specific influence of the HG gyrification pattern on speech-related functional lateralization of the PT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2 with effect sizes.

claim: No significant leftward PT lateralization was observed for speech perception and comprehension in the L2/R1 and L2/R2 groups.
source: As shown in Figure 2, significant leftward PT lateralization was observed for both speech perception and comprehension in the L1/R1 (Cohen's d: speech perception = 0.35, speech comprehension = 0.36) and L1/R2 (Cohen's d: speech perception = 0.52, speech comprehension = 0.57) groups but not in the L2/R1 and L2/R2 groups (Supplementary file 1a), suggesting a specific influence of the HG gyrification pattern on speech-related functional lateralization of the PT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: HG duplication was accompanied by decreased functional activation in the ipsilateral PT.
source: The results showed that HG duplication was largely accompanied by decreased functional activation in the ipsilateral PT, and the degree of such a decrease varied between the left and right PTs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: ODI showed consistent leftward asymmetry across all 4 HG gyrification pattern groups.
source: As shown in Figure 3, ODI and cortical thickness showed consistent leftward and rightward asymmetry across all 4 groups, suggesting a minimal influence of the HG gyrification pattern on the group-level PT asymmetry of these particular measures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cortical thickness showed consistent rightward asymmetry across all 4 HG gyrification pattern groups.
source: As shown in Figure 3, ODI and cortical thickness showed consistent leftward and rightward asymmetry across all 4 groups, suggesting a minimal influence of the HG gyrification pattern on the group-level PT asymmetry of these particular measures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Significant leftward asymmetry of PT surface area was observed in the L1/R1, L1/R2, and L2/R2 groups but not in the L2/R1 group.
source: Specifically, we observed (1) significant leftward asymmetry of PT surface area in the L1/R1, L1/R2, and L2/R2 groups (Cohen's d: L1/R1 = 0.42, L1/R2 = 1.48, L2/R2 = 0.73) but no asymmetry in the L2/R1 group
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with effect sizes.

claim: Significant leftward and rightward asymmetry of PT myelin content was observed only in the L1/R2 and L2/R1 groups.
source: (2) significant leftward and rightward asymmetry of PT myelin content only in the L1/R2 and L2/R1 groups (Cohen's d: L1/R2 = 0.58, L2/R1 = –0.68)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with effect sizes.

claim: Significant leftward NDI asymmetry was observed in the L1/R2 group but rightward NDI asymmetry in both the L1/R1 and L2/R1 groups.
source: (3) significant leftward NDI asymmetry in the L1/R2 group (Cohen's d: L1/R2 = 0.40) but rightward NDI asymmetry in both the L1/R1 and L2/R1 groups (Cohen's d: L1/R1 = –0.21, L2/R1 = –0.48) (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with effect sizes.

claim: HG duplication was accompanied by a decrease in surface area, myelin content, NDI, and ODI of the ipsilateral PT.
source: In addition, the comparison of these PT structural measures between subjects with sHG and dHG indicated that HG duplication was accompanied by a decrease in surface area, myelin content, NDI, and ODI of the ipsilateral PT, with the left and right PT also showing variable degrees of such a decrease (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The AI of PT speech comprehension activation was significantly correlated with picture vocabulary test scores (R = 0.10, PFWE = 0.047).
source: The AI of PT speech comprehension activation was found significantly correlated with picture vocabulary test scores (R = 0.10, PFWE = 0.047).
evidence: This correlation is explicitly stated in the Results section.

claim: No significant group effect (interaction with HG gyrification pattern) was observed for any functional-structural AI pair.
source: No significant group effect (i.e. the interaction with the HG gyrification pattern in the general linear model) was observed for any functional-structural AI pair.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structure-function association analysis.

claim: Functional AI of speech perception activation showed significant positive correlation with AI of myelin content (R = 0.26, PFWE = 1.22 × 10–13).
source: As shown in Figure 4, among these functional-structural pairs, the functional AI of speech perception activation showed significant positive correlations with the AIs of myelin content (R = 0.26, PFWE = 1.22 × 10–13), NDI (R = 0.13, PFWE = 2.00 × 10–3), and ODI (R = 0.22, PFWE = 1.75 × 10–9), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Functional AI of speech perception activation showed significant positive correlation with AI of NDI (R = 0.13, PFWE = 2.00 × 10–3).
source: As shown in Figure 4, among these functional-structural pairs, the functional AI of speech perception activation showed significant positive correlations with the AIs of myelin content (R = 0.26, PFWE = 1.22 × 10–13), NDI (R = 0.13, PFWE = 2.00 × 10–3), and ODI (R = 0.22, PFWE = 1.75 × 10–9), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Functional AI of speech perception activation showed significant positive correlation with AI of ODI (R = 0.22, PFWE = 1.75 × 10–9).
source: As shown in Figure 4, among these functional-structural pairs, the functional AI of speech perception activation showed significant positive correlations with the AIs of myelin content (R = 0.26, PFWE = 1.22 × 10–13), NDI (R = 0.13, PFWE = 2.00 × 10–3), and ODI (R = 0.22, PFWE = 1.75 × 10–9), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Functional AI of speech comprehension activation significantly correlated with AI of surface area (R = 0.21, PFWE = 2.66 × 10–9).
source: In contrast, functional AI of speech comprehension activation significantly correlated with the AIs of surface area (R = 0.21, PFWE = 2.66 × 10–9), myelin content (R = 0.20, PFWE = 4.66 × 10–8), and NDI (R = 0.11, PFWE = 1.47 × 10–2), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Functional AI of speech comprehension activation significantly correlated with AI of myelin content (R = 0.20, PFWE = 4.66 × 10–8).
source: In contrast, functional AI of speech comprehension activation significantly correlated with the AIs of surface area (R = 0.21, PFWE = 2.66 × 10–9), myelin content (R = 0.20, PFWE = 4.66 × 10–8), and NDI (R = 0.11, PFWE = 1.47 × 10–2), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Functional AI of speech comprehension activation significantly correlated with AI of NDI (R = 0.11, PFWE = 1.47 × 10–2).
source: In contrast, functional AI of speech comprehension activation significantly correlated with the AIs of surface area (R = 0.21, PFWE = 2.66 × 10–9), myelin content (R = 0.20, PFWE = 4.66 × 10–8), and NDI (R = 0.11, PFWE = 1.47 × 10–2), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Speech perception functional activation correlated positively with myelin content for the left PT (R = 0.16, PFWE = 6.47 × 10–5).
source: For speech perception, functional activation correlated positively with myelin content and ODI for either the left (myelin content: R = 0.16, PFWE = 6.47 × 10–5; ODI: R = 0.17, PFWE = 2.88 × 10–5) or right PT (myelin content: R = 0.20, PFWE = 1.30 × 10–7; ODI: R = 0.18, PFWE = 7.18 × 10–6), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Speech perception functional activation correlated positively with ODI for the left PT (R = 0.17, PFWE = 2.88 × 10–5).
source: For speech perception, functional activation correlated positively with myelin content and ODI for either the left (myelin content: R = 0.16, PFWE = 6.47 × 10–5; ODI: R = 0.17, PFWE = 2.88 × 10–5) or right PT (myelin content: R = 0.20, PFWE = 1.30 × 10–7; ODI: R = 0.18, PFWE = 7.18 × 10–6), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Speech perception functional activation correlated positively with myelin content for the right PT (R = 0.20, PFWE = 1.30 × 10–7).
source: For speech perception, functional activation correlated positively with myelin content and ODI for either the left (myelin content: R = 0.16, PFWE = 6.47 × 10–5; ODI: R = 0.17, PFWE = 2.88 × 10–5) or right PT (myelin content: R = 0.20, PFWE = 1.30 × 10–7; ODI: R = 0.18, PFWE = 7.18 × 10–6), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Speech perception functional activation correlated positively with ODI for the right PT (R = 0.18, PFWE = 7.18 × 10–6).
source: For speech perception, functional activation correlated positively with myelin content and ODI for either the left (myelin content: R = 0.16, PFWE = 6.47 × 10–5; ODI: R = 0.17, PFWE = 2.88 × 10–5) or right PT (myelin content: R = 0.20, PFWE = 1.30 × 10–7; ODI: R = 0.18, PFWE = 7.18 × 10–6), regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Speech perception activation showed significant correlation with surface area (R = –0.11, PFWE = 2.33 × 10–2) for the right PT but not the left PT.
source: Moreover, speech perception activation showed significant correlations with surface area (R = –0.11, PFWE = 2.33 × 10–2) and NDI (R = 0.14, PFWE = 2.16 × 10–3) for the right PT but not the left PT.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Speech perception activation showed significant correlation with NDI (R = 0.14, PFWE = 2.16 × 10–3) for the right PT but not the left PT.
source: Moreover, speech perception activation showed significant correlations with surface area (R = –0.11, PFWE = 2.33 × 10–2) and NDI (R = 0.14, PFWE = 2.16 × 10–3) for the right PT but not the left PT.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Speech comprehension functional activation significantly correlated with myelin content for the right PT (R = 0.16, PFWE = 2.59 × 10–5) but not the left PT.
source: Regarding speech comprehension, functional activation significantly correlated with myelin content for the right PT (R = 0.16, PFWE = 2.59 × 10–5) but not the left PT.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: A significant correlation was observed between functional activation of speech comprehension and NDI for the left PT (R = –0.12, PFWE = 1.62 × 10–2) but not the right PT.
source: We also observed a significant correlation between functional activation of speech comprehension and NDI for the left PT (R = –0.12, PFWE = 1.62 × 10–2) but not the right PT.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: There were only very few significant correlations among PT functional-structural pairs for the other six fMRI tasks.
source: As shown in Supplementary file 1b-1e, there were only very few significant correlations among the PT functional-structural pairs, therefore, supporting the specificity of our currently observed PT functional-structural couplings to the functional activation of auditory-language processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the specificity analysis.

claim: No significant interindividual correlation was found between PT structural AIs and speech-related functional AIs of the entire hemisphere.
source: The coupling analysis showed no significant interindividual correlation between PT structural AIs and speech-related functional AIs of the entire hemisphere or between PT structural measures and speech-related functional activation of the entire ipsilateral hemisphere (Supplementary file 1f-1i).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the spatial specificity analysis.

claim: PT structural measures or their asymmetries were coupled with PT-specific functional activation or their lateralization rather than with general functional activation or its lateralization in auditory-language processing.
source: Therefore, PT structural measures or their asymmetries were coupled with PT-specific functional activation or their lateralization rather than with general functional activation or its lateralization in auditory-language processing.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the Results section based on the specificity analyses.

claim: The planum temporale putatively plays an essential role in the functional lateralization of language processing.
source: As a well-known cortical area posterior to the Heschl's gyrus (HG), which includes most of the primary auditory cortex, the PT putatively plays an essential role in the functional lateralization of language processing (Albouy et al., 2020; Galaburda et al., 1978; Hickok and Poeppel, 2000; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; Moffat et al., 1998; Price, 2010; Steinmetz, 1996; Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: PT lateralization in functional activation during auditory- or language-related tasks has been well demonstrated.
source: its lateralization in functional activation during auditory- or language-related tasks has been well demonstrated (Albouy et al., 2020; Hunter et al., 2003; Pahs et al., 2013; Shapleske et al., 1999; Zatorre et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The PT shows distinct leftward asymmetries in a variety of structural aspects.
source: Additionally, the PT shows distinct leftward asymmetries in a variety of structural aspects, e.g., length, gray matter concentration/volume, surface area, cortical thickness, and columnar neuronal units, although the results might conflict between studies (Anderson et al., 1999; Bloom et al., 2013; Chance et al., 2008; Dorsaint-Pierre et al., 2006; Eckert et al., 2006; Fukutomi et al., 2018; Galuske et al., 2000; Greve et al., 2013; Josse et al., 2003; Knaus et al., 2006; Moffat et al., 1998; Ocklenburg et al., 2018; Schmitz et al., 2019; Sigalovsky et al., 2006; Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Examining the functional association of PT macrostructural asymmetries at the individual level almost always showed negative results, except for only a couple of studies.
source: Unexpectedly, examining the functional association of PT macrostructural asymmetries at the individual level almost always showed negative results, except for only a couple of studies demonstrating correlations between PT asymmetry of surface area and some non-PT-related indices of language lateralization, e.g., the lateralization of dichotic listening (Guadalupe et al., 2022; Hugdahl et al., 2003; Dos Santos Sequeira et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Recent studies have used novel MRI techniques to quantify PT microstructure on the level of axons or dendrites and revealed PT asymmetries in myelin content, neurite density, and neurite orientation dispersion.
source: Recent studies have used novel MRI techniques to quantify PT microstructure on the level of axons or dendrites and further revealed PT asymmetries in myelin content, neurite density, and neurite orientation dispersion (Fukutomi et al., 2018; Ocklenburg et al., 2018; Schmitz et al., 2019; Sigalovsky et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Postmortem work on the microstructure of the temporal cortex has led to the hypothesis that asymmetries in the organization of the intrinsic microcircuitry of the PT and other areas may be crucial for functional lateralization.
source: Importantly, postmortem work on the microstructure of the temporal cortex has led to the hypothesis that asymmetries in the organization of the intrinsic microcircuitry of the PT and other areas may be crucial for functional lateralization (Galuske et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Asymmetries in PT microstructure have been linked to electrophysiological correlates of auditory speech.
source: In line with this idea, asymmetries in PT microstructure have been linked to electrophysiological correlates of auditory speech, an indirect measure of functional language lateralization (Ocklenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Duplicated HG in the left or right hemisphere occurs substantially in healthy individuals, although less frequently than single HG.
source: Finally, duplicated HG (dHG) in the left or right hemisphere occurs substantially in healthy individuals, although less frequently than single HG (sHG) (Campain and Minckler, 1976; Leonard et al., 1998; Marie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: HG gyrification pattern is accompanied by significant differences in PT structural properties and their asymmetries compared with the single HG.
source: In particular, such an HG gyrification pattern is accompanied by significant differences in PT structural properties and their asymmetries compared with the single HG (Tzourio-Mazoyer and Mazoyer, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Cortical myelin content mainly reflects the degree of intracortical axonal myelination.
source: Here, cortical myelin content mainly reflects the degree of intracortical axonal myelination and was measured using a noninvasive T1w/T2w mapping approach (Glasser et al., 2016; Glasser and Van Essen, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Cortical NDI and ODI mainly represent the density of intracortical neurite and the complexity of dendritic arborization, respectively.
source: Cortical NDI and ODI mainly represent the density of intracortical neurite and the complexity of dendritic arborization, respectively (Ocklenburg et al., 2018), and were estimated using the diffusion MRI-based neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) model (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The anatomical leftward asymmetry of PT emerges at an early stage of life, prior to any environmental influences such as language exposure.
source: The anatomical leftward asymmetry of PT emerges at an early stage of life, prior to any environmental influences such as language exposure (Dubois et al., 2010; Witelson and Pallie, 1973).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Anomalies of PT asymmetries in surface area or thickness have been reported in various brain disorders with auditory or language deficits.
source: In concordance, anomalies of PT asymmetries in surface area or thickness have been reported in various brain disorders with auditory or language deficits, e.g., dyslexia, autism, and schizophrenia (Altarelli et al., 2014; Bloom et al., 2013; Floris et al., 2016; Hynd and Semrud-Clikeman, 1989; Knaus et al., 2018; Pahs et al., 2013; Sumich et al., 2002; Sumich et al., 2005; Vanderauwera et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The leftward structural asymmetry of the PT has been observed in multiple non-human primates, including chimpanzees, macaques, and baboons.
source: For example, the leftward structural asymmetry of the PT has been observed in multiple non-human primates, including chimpanzees, macaques, and baboons (Becker et al., 2024; Gannon et al., 1998; Xia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations supporting the claim.

claim: PT structural leftward asymmetry in newborn baboons could predict future development of communicative gestures.
source: Particularly, recent studies on baboons further demonstrated that PT structural leftward asymmetry in newborn baboons could predict future development of communicative gestures, implying a key role of PT structural asymmetry in the lateralized communication system for human and non-human brain evolution (Becker et al., 2021; Becker et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations supporting the claim.

claim: PT asymmetry in surface area was correlated with regional lateralization of language-related functional activation around the Sylvian fissure but not the activation of the PT.
source: For instance, PT asymmetry in surface area was correlated with regional lateralization of language-related functional activation around the Sylvian fissure but not the activation of the PT (Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: The present study provides the first empirical evidence of interindividual associations between functional and structural asymmetries within the PT.
source: Our present study provides the first empirical evidence of interindividual associations between functional and structural asymmetries within the PT, implying a functional pathway from PT structural asymmetry to PT functional lateralization to effective speech processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding of the study.

claim: The observed functional-structural coupling of PT asymmetries empirically proves the role of structural gray matter asymmetries in the functional lateralization of the same brain area.
source: In the context of brain asymmetries, our currently observed functional-structural coupling of PT asymmetries at the individual level empirically proves the role of structural gray matter asymmetries in the functional lateralization of the same brain area, supporting the compelling hypothesis that 'functional lateralization is guided by structural asymmetry' (Wada, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key interpretation of the findings.

claim: Specific microstructural asymmetry between bilateral PTs might cause less recruitment of the nondominant hemisphere in particular speech processing, therefore, resulting in more pronounced functional lateralization.
source: Specific microstructural asymmetry between bilateral PTs might cause less recruitment of the nondominant hemisphere in particular speech processing, therefore, resulting in more pronounced functional lateralization (Galaburda et al., 1990; Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possible explanation with citations.

claim: Higher myelin content and larger surface area in left PT potentially indicated more white matter connection with other language-related regions such as Broca's area.
source: Another possible explanation could be that higher myelin content and larger surface area in left PT potentially indicated more white matter connection with other language-related regions such as Broca's area, and therefore, is more involved in language tasks than its right homolog (Allendorfer et al., 2016; Catani et al., 2005; Giampiccolo and Duffau, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possible explanation with citations.

claim: Cortical areas with greater intracortical fiber density and more complex dendritic structures are likely accompanied by stronger local activation during the task.
source: These findings together indicate an important contribution of intracortical microcircuits to functional activity: cortical areas with greater intracortical fiber density and more complex dendritic structures are likely accompanied by stronger local activation during the task (Hall et al., 2003; Hunt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations supporting the claim.

claim: PT of the left hemisphere responded more strongly to lexical-semantic and syntactic aspects of sentence processing, whereas the right hemisphere demonstrated a greater involvement in the speech melody.
source: A number of studies substantiated that PT of the left hemisphere responded more strongly to lexical-semantic and syntactic aspects of sentence processing, whereas the right hemisphere demonstrated a greater involvement in the speech melody (Albouy et al., 2020; Meyer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The left arcuate fasciculus has been identified as a crucial structure for language function.
source: The left AF has been identified as a crucial structure for language function (Giampiccolo and Duffau, 2022; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Disruption to the left arcuate fasciculus has been linked to multimodal phonological and semantic deficits.
source: Disruption to this pathway has been linked to multimodal phonological and semantic deficits (Agosta et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Injuries in the right arcuate fasciculus did not affect language function.
source: while injuries in the right AF did not affect language function (Zeineh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: PT functional and structural asymmetries and their coupling might represent unique structural and functional information, independent of within-hemispheric PT measures.
source: This implied that PT functional and structural asymmetries and their coupling might represent unique structural and functional information, independent of within-hemispheric PT measures.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Both PT functional and structural AI showed an unimodal frequency distribution regardless of the HG gyrification pattern.
source: Regardless of the HG gyrification pattern, both PT functional and structural AI showed an unimodal frequency distribution (Guadalupe et al., 2022; Packheiser et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The occurrence of a left HG duplication was accompanied by a lack of the typically observed leftward asymmetry of PT activation, independent of the right HG duplication.
source: Intriguingly, the occurrence of a left HG duplication was accompanied by a lack of the typically observed leftward asymmetry of PT activation, independent of the right HG duplication, which is consistent with previous studies (Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2015; Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The functional-structural coupling of both PT asymmetries and within-hemispheric PT measures were not significantly affected by the HG gyrification pattern.
source: On the other hand, the functional-structural coupling of both PT asymmetries and within-hemispheric PT measures were not significantly affected by the HG gyrification pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a finding of the study.

claim: The association between specific PT functional and microstructural asymmetries provides direct empirical support for the contribution of structural asymmetry to functional lateralization of the same cortical area.
source: In conclusion, the association between specific PT functional and microstructural asymmetries provides direct empirical support for the contribution of structural asymmetry to functional lateralization of the same cortical area.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings highlight the critical role of microstructural PT asymmetries in auditory-language processing.
source: Moreover, the findings highlight the critical role of microstructural PT asymmetries in auditory-language processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: 72 subjects were excluded due to quality issues.
source: Due to quality issues (quality control codes A and B from the HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline), 72 subjects were excluded.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Only qualified right-handed subjects (Edinburgh Handedness questionnaire >20) were included in the analysis.
source: To control for the potential confounding effect of handedness, we included only qualified right-handed subjects (907 in total, Edinburgh Handedness questionnaire >20) in the analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: MRI data of all subjects were collected using the same 3T Siemens Skyra magnetic resonance machine at Washington University in St. Louis with a 32-channel head coil.
source: MRI data of all subjects were collected using the same 3T Siemens Skyra magnetic resonance machine at Washington University in St. Louis with a 32-channel head coil (Van Essen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation.

claim: The language processing task consisted of two runs containing four blocks of an auditory story task and four length-match blocks of an auditory math task.
source: The language processing task consisted of two runs containing four blocks of an auditory story task and four length-match blocks of an auditory math task.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the task paradigm.

claim: During the story blocks, participants were presented with auditory stories adapted from Aesop's fables, followed by a two-alternative forced-choice question about the topic of the story.
source: Specifically, during the story blocks, participants were presented with auditory stories adapted from Aesop's fables, followed by a two-alternative forced-choice question about the topic of the story.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the task paradigm.

claim: All MRI images were preprocessed using the HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline.
source: All MRI images were preprocessed using the HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline (Glasser et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation.

claim: The HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline provides the native pial and white surfaces that are resampled onto the standard 32 k_fs_LR mesh.
source: For each subject, the HCP minimal preprocessing pipeline provides the native pial and white surfaces that are resampled onto the standard 32 k_fs_LR mesh (~32 k vertices for each hemispheric surface).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The test-retest results of the HG gyrification pattern reached 100% consistency.
source: To evaluate the test-retest reproducibility of both manual operation and brain imaging, one rater (P.Q.) further determined the HG gyrification pattern and delineated the PT for the 43 test-retest HCP subjects who were rescanned (test-retest interval: 1–11 mo). The test-retest results of the HG gyrification pattern also reached 100% consistency.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The results of the HG gyrification pattern reached 100% consistency between the two raters.
source: To assess interrater reliability, the two raters both determined the HG gyrification pattern and delineated the PT for the same 20 randomly selected subjects. The results of the HG gyrification pattern reached 100% consistency.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: NDI is an estimated volume fraction of the intracellular microstructural environment in gray matter, with higher NDI indicating greater neurite density.
source: In the gray matter of the cerebral cortex, the NDI is an estimated volume fraction of the intracellular microstructural environment, with higher NDI indicating greater neurite density.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing NODDI measures.

claim: ODI is a measure of the alignment or dispersion of neurite, with higher ODI indicating more dispersed neurite and lower ODIs indicating more aligned neurite.
source: The ODI is a measure of the alignment or dispersion of neurite, with higher ODI indicating more dispersed neurite and lower ODIs indicating more aligned neurite (Jespersen et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing NODDI measures with citations.

claim: The significance level was set as p<0.05 after Bonferroni correction for each type of statistical analysis.
source: For each type of statistical analysis above, the significance level was set as p<0.05 after Bonferroni correction.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing statistical analysis.
